title: How a retaining wall is built

lines.en: Your house sits right at the bottom of a hill. And every time it rains, the hill slides a little closer to your bedroom.
First, you pull up samples of the soil, to find out how hard it's going to push.
So you build a thin wall. And the dirt just shoves it over, like a domino.
So you give it a wide foot underneath, and now the weight of the soil holds it down.
This is a footing.
But the hill can still push the whole thing forward, sliding it like a hockey puck.
So you add a concrete tooth under the footing that bites into the ground.
This is a shear key.
Now, for real. You place steel bars that run from the footing up into the wall, so they work as one piece.
You set up wooden forms, pour the concrete, and shake it, so no air bubbles get trapped inside.
Then you keep it wet for days while it hardens, so it doesn't crack.
This is curing.
But when it rains, water piles up behind the wall, and pushes even harder than the dirt.
So you leave little pipes through the wall to let the water out.
These are weep holes.
Right behind the wall, you add gravel and a pipe full of holes, so the water runs down and out.
Then you fill it back in with soil, one packed layer at a time.
Up the hill, you dig a channel that catches the rain before it ever reaches the wall.
And you plant the slope, so the roots hold the dirt together.
Congratulations! You have built a retaining wall.
